slides.title: Two Separate Guarantees
slides.lead:
Cloud storage carries two risks: data loss forever, or the service simply not responding right now
Durability covers survival of data over time; availability covers whether the service responds to requests

points.text: Durability measures whether stored bytes survive hardware failure, corruption or disasters over time
Availability measures whether the storage service answers a read or write request now

slides.notes: Open by separating the two fears: losing data forever versus not reaching it right now. Say the locker example aloud before naming the terms. Interviewers often test this exact distinction, so stress that durability is about loss and availability is about uptime.

slides.title: Two Separate Guarantees

points.text: An object can be perfectly durable yet briefly unreachable during maintenance or an outage
A highly available service can still lose data permanently if its durability safeguards fail

slides.notes: Open by separating the two fears: losing data forever versus not reaching it right now. Say the locker example aloud before naming the terms. Interviewers often test this exact distinction, so stress that durability is about loss and availability is about uptime.

slides.label: Analogy: a bank account and an ATM
slides.title: Two Separate Guarantees
slides.notes: TR analogy: Your money in a bank account stays safe even when the nearby ATM is out of service. The money not being lost is durability; the ATM working right now to give you cash is availability. In the same way, a storage service can keep data perfectly safe while being briefly unreachable.

slides.title: Durability And Uptime
slides.lead: Providers protect data with redundancy and promise uptime through a Service Level Agreement (SLA), so the two guarantees are engineered and stated differently

points.text: Durability: checksums detect corruption
And erasure coding spreads data fragments across at least three Availability Zones
S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) yearly durability
A loss probability, not a zero-loss promise

slides.notes: Explain eleven nines as roughly one object in a hundred billion lost per year, not zero loss. Then convert the 99.9% SLA into about 8.76 hours of downtime yearly. Stress that design targets and SLA numbers differ, and that SLA breaches pay credits, not cash. Exam angle: convert an SLA percentage into allowed downtime.

slides.title: Durability And Uptime

points.text: Availability: promised as monthly uptime in an SLA; missing it earns service credits, not a refund
S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability
But its SLA promises 99.9%, about 8.76 hours of downtime a year

slides.notes: Explain eleven nines as roughly one object in a hundred billion lost per year, not zero loss. Then convert the 99.9% SLA into about 8.76 hours of downtime yearly. Stress that design targets and SLA numbers differ, and that SLA breaches pay credits, not cash. Exam angle: convert an SLA percentage into allowed downtime.

slides.title: Durability Vs Availability Numbers
slides.lead:
AWS publishes separate durability and availability numbers because each guards against a different failure
The storage class chosen decides which guarantee weakens for a lower price
slides.notes: Point out that durability barely changes across classes, while the availability SLA drops for the single-AZ option. Ask students why durability stays high even in one AZ — it measures bit-level survival, not reachability. This table reappears when comparing storage classes on cost.

slides.title: Checking The Documents
slides.lead: Every AWS storage service publishes its durability design and availability SLA on a public page, and the console shows which storage class an object uses

points.text: AWS publishes a separate SLA per service, listing uptime commitment and credit percentages
Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes and other storage services also have published guarantees
Checking the written guarantee first avoids assuming a stronger promise than exists

slides.notes: Show where the storage class field sits in the S3 console, linking it to the durability and SLA promise. Mention these are legal SLA pages, not marketing claims. Note the promise still needs a mechanism to be kept.

slides.title: Checking The Documents
slides.lead: These published numbers describe only the promise; replication across facilities is the mechanism that actually keeps data meeting it
slides.notes: Show where the storage class field sits in the S3 console, linking it to the durability and SLA promise. Mention these are legal SLA pages, not marketing claims. Note the promise still needs a mechanism to be kept.

slides.title: Copies And Consistency
slides.lead:
Providers also protect data by keeping multiple live copies, called replication
Consistency models decide how soon every copy shows the same value

points.text: Within-region replication keeps extra copies across separate data centres in one region
Cross-region replication copies data into an entirely different region for wider protection
Consistency models define how quickly a written copy becomes visible to later readers

slides.notes: Set up replication as the next layer above durability and availability. Say plainly that more copies mean more protection, but copies can disagree for a short while. Point out the two scopes shown before moving into each one.

slides.title: Sync Vs Async Copies
slides.lead: Replication keeps a duplicate of changing data, copied either synchronously or asynchronously

points.text: Synchronous replication confirms a write only after the standby copy also has it
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication for its standby copy within a region
Asynchronous replication confirms the write first, then copies it to the other side
Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) uses asynchronous replication, causing a short lag

slides.notes: Open RDS Multi-AZ mentally as the within-region example before naming S3 CRR for cross-region. Stress that sync trades a little latency for safety, while async trades a little freshness for reach. Interview hook: ask why RDS Multi-AZ is synchronous but read replicas are not.

slides.title: Sync Vs Async Copies
slides.notes: Open RDS Multi-AZ mentally as the within-region example before naming S3 CRR for cross-region. Stress that sync trades a little latency for safety, while async trades a little freshness for reach. Interview hook: ask why RDS Multi-AZ is synchronous but read replicas are not.

slides.title: Sync Vs Async Copies

points.text: Cross-region copies also place data physically closer to users worldwide
Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables replicate one table across chosen regions for reads and writes

slides.notes: Open RDS Multi-AZ mentally as the within-region example before naming S3 CRR for cross-region. Stress that sync trades a little latency for safety, while async trades a little freshness for reach. Interview hook: ask why RDS Multi-AZ is synchronous but read replicas are not.

slides.title: Strong Vs Eventual
slides.lead:
A consistency model defines how soon readers see an updated value after a write
Cloud storage typically offers two models: strong consistency and eventual consistency

points.text: Strong consistency guarantees a read right after a write returns the latest value
Eventual consistency allows a brief delay before all copies agree
Eventual consistency trades instant freshness for lower latency and wider reach

slides.notes: Explain strong consistency first because it matches everyday expectation, then show why eventual consistency is accepted for speed and reach. Mention S3's strong consistency as a point most learners get wrong in interviews. Keep the chat board picture in mind while explaining the lag.

slides.title: Strong Vs Eventual

points.text: Amazon S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for all object operations today
Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables default to eventual consistency for reads across regions
DynamoDB still offers a strongly consistent read option within a single region

slides.notes: Explain strong consistency first because it matches everyday expectation, then show why eventual consistency is accepted for speed and reach. Mention S3's strong consistency as a point most learners get wrong in interviews. Keep the chat board picture in mind while explaining the lag.

slides.label: Analogy: a principal's notice
slides.title: Strong Vs Eventual
slides.notes: TR analogy: A school principal's notice appears instantly on the office board, but photocopies pinned on each wing's board take a few minutes to catch up — just as eventual consistency lets distant copies lag briefly before matching the original.

slides.label: Choosing The Right Fit

props.title: Choosing The Right Fit
props.lead:
Choosing replication scope and a consistency model builds on the durability and availability promise made earlier
The same balance of cost, latency and freshness carries into the next storage tier decision

slides.notes: Walk the table row by row, linking scope, mode and consistency so the pattern stays visible rather than memorised. Note that the same trade-off reappears when choosing a storage tier. This slide is a recap table, not a new idea.

slides.title: Hot Cool Archive
slides.lead:
Storage tiering moves data across classes priced by access frequency, trading retrieval speed for cost
Cloud providers group these into hot, cool and archive tiers

points.text: Hot tier keeps frequently accessed data on costly, instantly available storage like Amazon S3 Standard
Cool tier stores infrequently accessed data cheaper, with a small retrieval fee, like S3 Standard-IA
Archive tier stores rarely accessed data cheapest, with retrieval delayed minutes to hours, like S3 Glacier

slides.notes: Introduce tiering as grouping storage classes by access frequency, not data type. Mention all three tiers together, noting this mirrors the hot/cool/archive diagram. Flag that interviewers often ask which AWS class belongs to which tier.

slides.title: Retrieval Cost Trade-Off
slides.lead:
Most data is read often soon after creation and rarely later, so paying premium rates forever wastes money
Tiering matches storage class to access pattern, so cost falls as access frequency drops

points.text: Retrieval time rises from milliseconds to hours, moving hot to archive
Per-gigabyte storage price drops sharply moving from hot to archive
Retrieval fees per request or gigabyte rise from hot to archive

slides.notes: Explain the trade-off as an economic one: speed costs money, so storage should not pay for speed it never uses. Use the library analogy verbally, pointing at the three-tier diagram while narrating it. Mention this trade-off is a favourite interview question on storage cost optimisation.

slides.label: Analogy: clothes and documents at home
slides.title: Retrieval Cost Trade-Off
slides.notes: TR analogy: At home, daily-wear clothes stay in the wardrobe for instant use, winter clothes go into a suitcase in the loft that takes a few minutes to bring down, and old documents go into a bank locker that needs a trip to fetch. In the same way, hot, cool and archive tiers trade instant access for lower storage cost.

slides.title: Standard And Infrequent
slides.lead:
In Amazon S3, the hot tier is S3 Standard and the cool tier is S3 Standard-IA
Both store data in the same region but price it differently based on read frequency

points.text: S3 Standard offers millisecond retrieval with no retrieval fee
S3 Standard-IA offers millisecond retrieval but charges a per-gigabyte retrieval fee

slides.notes: Show the storage class dropdown in the S3 console when uploading or editing an object. Cool-tier storage costs less per gigabyte, but the retrieval fee only pays off below roughly monthly access. Mention One Zone-IA's single-zone trade-off as a likely interview point.

slides.title: Standard And Infrequent

points.text: S3 One Zone-IA costs less than Standard-IA but keeps data in a single AZ
So losing that AZ means losing the data
A hot-tier example is an active website asset; a cool-tier example is a monthly report

slides.notes: Show the storage class dropdown in the S3 console when uploading or editing an object. Cool-tier storage costs less per gigabyte, but the retrieval fee only pays off below roughly monthly access. Mention One Zone-IA's single-zone trade-off as a likely interview point.

slides.title: Glacier Retrieval Options
slides.lead: The archive tier itself splits into variants that trade retrieval speed for even lower cost, used for data kept mainly for compliance or long-term backup rather than active use

points.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: millisecond access, priced above deeper archive classes
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval returns data within minutes to a few hours
S3 Glacier Deep Archive returns data within about twelve hours, the lowest-cost class
Archive classes charge for a minimum storage duration, even if deleted early

slides.notes: Explain that archive variants are tiers within the archive tier, not a separate fourth tier. Show that the S3 console's lifecycle and storage-class settings choose the archive class. Exam hook: Deep Archive is cheapest but slowest; Instant Retrieval is fastest but costliest.

slides.title: Why They Exist
slides.lead:
Tracking the age of millions of objects manually is impossible at scale
A lifecycle policy is a rule set that automatically moves or deletes objects once they reach a set age

points.text: A rule applies to a bucket, prefix, or tag
Each rule holds two kinds of action: tier transition or expiration
AWS Console: S3 bucket's Management tab, under Lifecycle rules, configures this
Rules are evaluated on a daily cycle by the storage service itself

slides.notes: Explain lifecycle policies as the automation that removes manual tier management at scale. Mention the S3 Console location for configuring rules. Exam hook: lifecycle rules run automatically inside the storage service, with no application code involved.

slides.label: Analogy: files in an office
slides.title: Why They Exist
slides.notes: TR analogy: In an office, active files stay on the desk, files older than six months are moved to the record room, and files older than seven years are shredded as per company policy, without anyone deciding each time. In the same way, a lifecycle policy automatically moves objects to cheaper tiers and deletes them once they reach a set age.

slides.title: Moving By Age
slides.lead:
A transition rule moves an object to a cheaper class once it reaches a set age, keeping its key
A minimum storage duration applies, since early moves can cost more than staying put

points.text: Transition age: S3 Standard moves to Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) after 30 days, for example
Further ageing can move the object again, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive

slides.notes: Walk through the timeline bar showing objects cooling tier by tier. Key cost point: moving data out before the minimum storage duration can cost more than leaving it in place. Interview hook: ask why providers enforce this minimum duration.

slides.title: Moving By Age

points.text: Early-move penalty: extra days are billed at the old class's rate, not the new one
A single rule can chain several transitions in sequence on one filter

slides.notes: Walk through the timeline bar showing objects cooling tier by tier. Key cost point: moving data out before the minimum storage duration can cost more than leaving it in place. Interview hook: ask why providers enforce this minimum duration.

slides.title: Deleting By Age
slides.lead:
An expiration rule deletes an object once it crosses a set age
In a versioned bucket, this only adds a delete marker, so a separate noncurrent-version rule is needed to remove old copies

points.text: Current-version age limits are usually set well beyond the last planned tier transition
Noncurrent-version expiration: clears older versions kept behind by bucket versioning
Incomplete multipart upload cleanup: removes abandoned partial uploads after a few days
Expiration frees storage cost entirely, unlike a transition, which only lowers it

slides.notes: Separate expiration from transition: one removes cost entirely, the other only lowers it. Note that noncurrent-version expiration only matters once versioning is already switched on. Exam hook: ask what happens to old versions in a versioned bucket with no expiration rule set.

slides.title: One Object Traced
slides.lead: A 2 GB log file uploaded to S3 Standard moves to Standard-IA at day 30, Glacier at day 90, and expires at day 365, all under one combined lifecycle rule
slides.notes: Trace the log file row by row, showing transition and expiration inside one combined rule. Note retrieval time rising as cost falls at each step. Interview hook: ask the restore cost if the file is read back on day 95.

slides.title: One Object Traced
slides.lead: Lifecycle policies manage cost across an object's working life, while backup and disaster-recovery planning protects against the one event a lifecycle rule never anticipates: unplanned data loss

chips.text: Never Anticipated By A Lifecycle Rule

slides.notes: Trace the log file row by row, showing transition and expiration inside one combined rule. Note retrieval time rising as cost falls at each step. Interview hook: ask the restore cost if the file is read back on day 95.

slides.title: Types Of Backups
slides.lead:
Storage replication guards against disk failure but not deletion, corruption or ransomware
A backup strategy keeps separate recoverable copies, trading storage and restore time for simplicity

points.text: Full backup copies all data every time, giving fastest restore but highest storage cost
Incremental backup copies only data changed since last backup, saving storage but slowing restores

slides.notes: Explain that replication guards against hardware failure, not accidental or malicious deletion. Mention that AWS Backup centralises scheduling across EBS, RDS and S3. Interviewers often ask the difference between incremental and differential backup, so stress that distinction.

slides.title: Types Of Backups

points.text: Differential backup copies all changes since last full backup, balancing storage cost against restore speed
Snapshot-based backup captures a point-in-time image of a volume or database for near-instant recovery

slides.notes: Explain that replication guards against hardware failure, not accidental or malicious deletion. Mention that AWS Backup centralises scheduling across EBS, RDS and S3. Interviewers often ask the difference between incremental and differential backup, so stress that distinction.

slides.title: Measuring Recovery Targets
slides.lead:
Disaster recovery answers two questions: how much data can be lost, and how long the system can stay down
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) caps data loss; Recovery Time Objective (RTO) caps downtime

points.text: A four-hour RPO requires backups at least every four hours
A one-hour RTO requires full recovery within one hour of failure
Lower RPO and RTO values cost more, needing frequent backups and standby capacity
Payment and order databases target near-zero RPO and RTO; archives tolerate higher values

slides.notes: Walk through the two questions RPO and RTO answer before naming them. AWS Backup and monitoring dashboards report actual RPO and RTO against targets. Interviewers often ask for a one-line definition distinguishing RPO from RTO.

slides.label: Analogy: a shop owner's notebook
slides.title: Measuring Recovery Targets
slides.notes: TR analogy: A shop owner copies the day's sales into a notebook every evening. If the billing computer crashes, at most one day of sales records is lost (RPO), and the time taken to set up a new computer and start billing again is the downtime (RTO). In the same way, RPO limits how much data can be lost and RTO limits how long the system stays down.

slides.title: Backup To Standby
slides.lead:
Disaster recovery (DR) plans sit along a cost-versus-speed spectrum: spending more on standby infrastructure buys a faster recovery
Three common patterns occupy different points on this spectrum

points.text: Backup-restore rebuilds infrastructure from scratch, the cheapest and slowest pattern
Pilot light keeps a minimal core, like a database, always running
Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy continuously

slides.notes: Name all three patterns together first so the full spectrum is visible. Note that AWS builds these using AWS Backup, read replicas, Auto Scaling and Route 53 failover routing. Ask which pattern suits a database-only workload as a quick check.

slides.title: Backup To Standby

points.text: Each pattern trades a higher standby cost for a lower recovery time objective

slides.notes: Name all three patterns together first so the full spectrum is visible. Note that AWS builds these using AWS Backup, read replicas, Auto Scaling and Route 53 failover routing. Ask which pattern suits a database-only workload as a quick check.

slides.title: Rebuild After Disaster
slides.lead: Backup-restore relies entirely on the backups built earlier: no standby servers run in the disaster recovery (DR) region until a disaster is actually declared

points.text: Snapshots and database dumps sit in a separate region, ready for restore
After a disaster, new infrastructure is built from scratch and the latest backup restored onto it

slides.notes: Stress that backup-restore spends nothing on standby compute, making it the slowest to recover. Name AWS Backup and cross-region S3 copies as the services behind it. Note the cost-versus-speed trade-off, since it recurs across every DR pattern.

slides.title: Rebuild After Disaster

points.text: RTO is high, often hours, since compute, network and app setup follow the failure
This pattern is cheapest; AWS Backup and S3 storage costs run even without failures

slides.notes: Stress that backup-restore spends nothing on standby compute, making it the slowest to recover. Name AWS Backup and cross-region S3 copies as the services behind it. Note the cost-versus-speed trade-off, since it recurs across every DR pattern.

slides.title: Core Always Running
slides.lead: Pilot light keeps only the smallest essential core, typically a database, continuously replicating into the disaster recovery (DR) region, while the compute layers above it stay switched off until needed

points.text: A replicated database, such as a read replica, stays live and synced with production
Application and web servers exist only as stopped machine images
Failover starts the stopped servers and redirects traffic, cutting recovery time to minutes
Running cost stays lower than warm standby since only the core runs continuously

slides.notes: Pilot light keeps only the core data layer alive, not the full application stack. AWS mechanics: an always-on database replica with stopped EC2 images ready to launch. Interviews often ask how pilot light differs from warm standby in what stays running.

slides.title: Scaled-Down Full Copy
slides.lead: Warm standby runs a complete, scaled-down copy of the production system in the DR region, kept ready to serve traffic at lower cost

points.text: Every tier, web, application and database, runs continuously at reduced capacity in DR
Failover usually scales the standby to full capacity and redirects traffic within minutes

slides.notes: Contrast warm standby with pilot light: here every tier runs, not just the database. Mention Auto Scaling groups at low minimum capacity and failover routing as the AWS mechanics. Ask what happens if scaled-down capacity cannot absorb full production load after failover.

slides.title: Scaled-Down Full Copy

points.text: RTO is lower than pilot light since the whole stack is live
RPO is similar, as both replicate data continuously
Running cost is higher since compute runs continuously across every tier, not just the core

slides.notes: Contrast warm standby with pilot light: here every tier runs, not just the database. Mention Auto Scaling groups at low minimum capacity and failover routing as the AWS mechanics. Ask what happens if scaled-down capacity cannot absorb full production load after failover.

slides.label: Choosing A Pattern

props.title: Choosing A Pattern
props.lead:
An order-processing database allows at most 5 minutes of data loss and must recover within 10 minutes of a regional outage
Checking these targets against the three patterns shows which one qualifies
props.note: Warm standby is the only pattern whose typical figures comfortably clear both the 5-minute RPO and the 10-minute RTO target, at the cost of running a scaled-down full stack continuously

slides.notes: Walk through the table to show why only warm standby clears both targets. Stress that these RPO and RTO figures are business decisions, not fixed technical constants. Interview questions often give an RPO/RTO pair and ask which DR pattern fits, as practised here.
